title: Damning data: stats that show Michael Carrick’s luck was bound to run out | Andrew Beasley
author: Andrew Beasley
text:
Favourable conditions and the rub of the green were behind Manchester United’s successful finish to last season

Manchester United have been the third‑best team in the Premier League with Michael Carrick as their head coach. It is some effort for his job to be so under threat when only Arsenal (57 points) and Manchester City (56) have been more productive than United (46) during the 45-year-old’s tenure.

The tally obscures pertinent facts. United topping the Premier League during his 17‑match interim spell last season is irrelevant when they sit 16th with no win in eight games in all competitions this season. Losing narrowly against City is one thing, but three-goal defeats by Como and Bournemouth will surely spell managerial change.

Carrick can point to a degree of misfortune this season. Conceding stoppage-time equalisers to Everton and Tottenham was costly, although they also required an 89th-minute goal to avoid losing at Fulham , who were winless at the time.

Opta’s expected points model suggests United have earned 3.8 points fewer than their underlying statistical performances merit in 2026-27. Only three clubs are further adrift of where they can reasonably expect to be.

Equally, United’s expected position of 10th is hardly befitting a club whose net transfer spend this summer topped all those outside the Premier League bar Real Madrid, even before we consider their annual revenue and illustrious history. Their par level remains uninspiring.

If they have been a touch unlucky with results, it was almost an inevitable outcome. United outperformed their expected points by 12.7 in Carrick’s share of 2025-26, 7.6 more than any other club. Such fortune was never going to last, as any back office paying the remotest attention to data would know. Poor recruitment in the summer increased the likelihood of a slump.

The run of results appeared as unsustainable as it has proven. Eight of United’s 12 league wins under Carrick last season were by one goal. In that time, only Napoli (nine) had more such victories in Europe’s big five leagues. The expected goal margin was no more than 0.6 in United’s favour in five of those eight victories and they lost the xG by about 0.6 in their draws at West Ham and Sunderland. A lot of coin-flips went in their favour.

United’s woes are not simply the result of luck turning against them. They are incapable of breaking down teams when dominating the ball. Something that seemed insurmountable for Ole Gunnar Solskjær has also hampered Carrick. Meet the new overpromoted club legend, same as the old overpromoted club legend.

In Carrick’s first game, United won a Manchester derby despite having 32% possession. They were similarly ball-averse in victories against Liverpool (38%), Chelsea (40%) and Arsenal (43%) last season. Yet they have drawn blanks against Hull and Bournemouth in 2026-27 despite having 72% and 63% possession respectively. They were also unable to break down City when having a man advantage for three-quarters of the contest and 55% possession.

United lead the division for shots, but no team have had a higher proportion of their efforts from outside the penalty area, which explains why their non‑penalty expected goals per shot average is the second‑worst in the Premier League.

It is therefore fair to question Carrick’s tactical blueprint, as Bruno Fernandes did after defeat by Como . “Whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don’t run, and you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you ain’t going to win,” was Carrick’s response to his captain’s comments. A look at United’s physical data justifies his concern.

It is important to remember there is little correlation between distance covered and success . Arsenal lead the league for kilometres per match this season (119.4) but Fulham (119.0) are second. United are third-bottom, though their 112.3km per game average is up on the 102.2km they posted for Carrick in 2025-26.

Far more notable is the shift in sprints. Data from Gradient Sports shows United’s outfield players are averaging fewer sprints per 90 minutes than they did under Carrick last season. Youri Tielemans is not just below his figure for Aston Villa in 2025-26, he is barely at the level Casemiro offered despite being five years his junior.

The increase in average possession from 49.1% under Carrick last season to 56.7% may partially explain why United are sprinting less. However, City lead the Premier League for possession (64.7%) and average marginally fewer sprints than United, while Arsenal have the second-most ball (61.1%) and sprint more often. It seems unlikely United’s sprinting decline is entirely by design.

Have the players stopped trying for Carrick? Or do they simply no longer have the advantage of free weeks thanks to the Champions League qualification his success brought? Wherever the truth lies, intensity has dropped. The favourable circumstances of last season have gone and Carrick does not look up to the task of navigating a far more challenging campaign.

title: Michael Carrick attends Manchester United training ground as club discuss his fate
author: Jamie Jackson
text:
Head coach arrives to watch under-21s play

Bruno Fernandes likes Instagram post about loyalty

Michael Carrick was at Manchester United’s training ground on Monday afternoon as elsewhere at the ­Carrington base Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and Omar ­Berrada, the chief executive officer, deliberated over whether to sack the head coach.

Carrick arrived at 1.50pm to watch the under-21s play a behind‑closed-doors game.

Wilcox and Berrada met at Carrington early on Monday morning after United’s 3-0 defeat against ­Bournemouth on Sunday at Old Trafford that left Carrick’s job in the balance . Wilcox departed just before 5pm and Carrick left shortly after.

The defeat made it eight games without a win for Carrick’s side, who have two victories all season. United are in 16th in the Premier League, just a point above the relegation zone.

If the 45-year-old Carrick is removed, Eddie Howe remains ­Wilcox’s preferred candidate , with contact between the parties understood to have been made. The former Newcastle ­manager is open to taking up the position, ­subject to negotiations.

Howe, 48, would be less expensive to recruit than Unai Emery, another admired manager, because Aston Villa would demand around £20m in compensation for the ­Spaniard.

Julian Nagelsmann, the ­former Germany and Bayern Munich head coach, is highly regarded by ­Christopher ­Vivell, United’s director of ­recruitment, who is believed to have sounded out his fellow ­German. The pair previously worked together at RB Leipzig.

Wilcox’s view may hold more sway with Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who ­controls football policy at United. Antonio Conte, who left Napoli in the summer, is another who may be in the frame.

Carrick dropped Bruno Fernandes for the Bournemouth defeat for what he claimed were “pure football reasons”. This came after the 32‑year‑old criticised Carrick for his tactics in the 4-1 capitulation at Como in the ­Champions League last Wednesday. The United captain was an unused substi­tute and was booed, along with other players, by fans in the ­Stretford End at the end of the defeat against Marco Rose’s side.

On Monday Fernandes liked an ­Instagram post that said: “Never push a loyal person to the point where they no longer care.” The post also said: “The person holding everything together is usually the one nobody thinks to check on.”

Ineos, which is owned by ­Ratcliffe, has reportedly put FC ­Lausanne‑Sport up for sale. Ineos declined to comment when contacted by the ­Guardian. ­Lausanne-Sport are bottom of the top division in Switzerland.

title: This Is the Future of Gravel Bikes: 6 Bikes Tested Head to Head on a 100km Ride
author: Will Tracy
text:
Our quest to find the future of gravel bikes at the Velo Field Test has taken us on a long journey. We’ve test ridden six bikes that couldn’t be more different on a first impressions loop , and put the bikes through a series of head to head challenges . Now it’s time to test these bikes in the way that really matters: a big ride. In this final episode, we’re riding 100 kilometers (62 miles) up British Columbia’s Sea to Sky corridor from Squamish to Whistler.

In a discipline where people regularly ride hundreds of kilometers in one go, 100 isn’t the most insane distance. But it’s what’s contained in that distance that’s the challenge. Mike Levy has wracked the depths of his local knowledge to devise a course that hits all sorts of gravel terrain, and will push Josh and Logan to their limits as they in turn find the limits of the bikes.

There’s champagne gravel, gravel that is more aptly described as large rocks, steep climbs, technical single track, and some connectors on paved roads for good measure. Each of our six test bikes gets a chance to shine, and will also have its weaknesses glaringly exposed.

We have three riders and six bikes, so in order to test every bike on the ride, each tester will be switching out bikes at the halfway point. Who gets to pick what? Well we settled that in the most obvious way possible: go-karts. We found out that while Logan has Josh beat in a gravel race, Josh’s background hanging around L.A.’s underground street racing scene gave him the upper hand with track times. And that means he gets to pick what bikes Logan rides.

After hundreds of kilometers of riding and a series of head-to-head challenges, Levy, Josh, and Logan sit down to debate what the future of gravel bikes really looks like. Are bigger wheels the answer? Does suspension belong on gravel bikes? Are we sacrificing too much capability in the pursuit of speed? And most importantly, which of these six bikes would each tester actually take home?

The all-rounder: race it or go adventuring.

Specification: Giant Revolt Advanced SL 0, SRAM Red XPLR Tire clearance, claimed: 53mm Weight (tested size): 7.85kg/17.3lbs (ML)

Specification : Factor Sarana, SRAM Force XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 56mm Weight (tested size) : 9.58kg/21.12lbs (Medium)

Specification : Argon 18 Anti Matter + SRAM RED XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 55mm Weight (tested size) : 8.5kg/18.74lbs (Medium)

Specification : Obed GVR, SRAM Red XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 56mm Weight (tested size) : 9.12kg/20.1lbs (Medium)

Specification : Pivot Les SL Drop Bar, SRAM GX Eagle Transmission 12-Speed Tire clearance, claimed : 29 x 2.4″ Weight (tested size) : 9.78kg/21.56lbs (Medium)

The 32er. How much difference do big wheels make?

Specification : Salsa Fargo 32 Ti, SRAM GX Eagle Transmission Tire clearance, claimed : 60mm Weight (tested size) : 9.48kg/20.9lbs (Medium)

To settle the debate about the future of gravel once and for all (or perhaps muddy it more than ever), we’ve assembled three test riders who, like the bikes, couldn’t be more different.

Reformed mountain biker turned drop-bar obsessive Mike Levy leads the charge, bringing a technical, rowdy background and a preference for chunkier roads and adventuring far off the beaten path—on Earth and beyond.

He’s joined by Velo’s in-house team of tech editors. Josh Ross likes to ride long distances as efficiently as possible—catch him pedaling all day and night across the gravel roads of the Pacific Northwest and beyond. He’s all about pushing his personal boundaries, and finding the equipment that will help him go the extra mile (or extra 200 miles).

Having once finished 18th overall at the Unbound 200, Logan Jones-Wilkins can’t stop thinking about going fast and squeezing every drop of performance from gravel gear. But when he’s not mixing it up in the pointy end of races, he likes his gravel bike to be a medium for adventuring into the unknown.

That’s three different approaches to gravel, and, naturally, their takes are as varied as the riders themselves. Can they settle their differences and agree on anything? We may have to resort to some good ol’ fashioned tactics to resolve things—which may or may not mean go-kart racing.

To put these bikes to the ultimate test (and the riders too), we’ve taken everyone to the outdoor playground that is Squamish, British Columbia. Finding out the future of gravel means pushing bikes to their limits, so we’ve found a mix of terrain from single track to washboard fire roads to do just that.

We’re stress testing the bikes to get the most possible out of them. In this first episode, we’ve put together a test loop that takes our riders on a smattering of every kind of terrain one might consider gravel, from champagne roads, to loamy dirt trails, to slightly technical, rocky single track, and we’ve got climbing and descending for all of the above.

To keep our testing focused on the bikes themselves, we’ve brought in control tires, 50mm Schwalbe G-One RX tires run at the same tire pressure, mounted to Easton EC90 ALX wheels .

Velo Field Test wouldn’t happen without the support of these sponsors. A big thank you to Endura for providing kits and helmets, Schwalbe for tires, and Easton for wheels!

A special thank you to the crew who made this Velo Field Test a reality!

There’s more to come from the Velo Gravel Bike Field Test! We argue in depth about the future of gravel bikes on our podcast roundtable discussion, plus we have individual reviews for every single bike on test.

title: Football Daily | United’s cycle of hope followed by failure claims another patsy in Carrick
author: John Brewin
text:
By the time you’re reading this, Michael Carrick will probably have been sacked . If not, it will happen soon enough. Who to blame? The people have spoken. Acknowledging supporters after Manchester United did their usual and got pumped by Bournemouth to send the latest patsy handed the reins towards the door marked “Do One”, Carrick was applauded by the Stretford End, and Old Trafford’s stands east, south and north. A proud man walking, as Claudio Ranieri once described the fate of the manager who knows the end is approaching. Among the paying public, on the long list of those held responsible for the latest betrayal of a legend, Carrick is towards the bottom. If even on it. Those heading the list felt their ears burn in a atmosphere crackling with mutiny.

Time for The Daily Star to buy a lettuce from Tesco and place it against Michael Carrick – Krishna Moorthy.

Michael Carrick will probably have been politely asked to fold up his umbrella permanently by the time today’s Football Daily is published, but in the meantime I can’t help but wonder what sort of a brolly he owns, if it keeps other people dry, but not him? And why did he buy something that doesn’t perform the basic function for which it is purchased – isn’t that Jason Wilcox’s job? – Phil Taverner.

So, in the upcoming inevitable search for yet another Messiah, we’ve almost completed the cycle twice of the Dutchman Van Gaal to the Portuguese Mourinho to the ex-Ferguson player who knows the club Solskjær to German pressing-obsessive Rangnick and back round to van Nistelrooy, then Amorim and Carrick … which suggests that next chump to end up with a bunch of players who only try until the end of the season under a new manager and then give up completely and leave the manager to take the fall for their (and the board/owner) failings will be a German. Good luck in 2027/28 trying to get this mob to press, or even just make a basic effort and pass 5-10 yards to a teammate under no pressure , Julian Nagelsmann! – Noble Francis.

Is it too late to nominate Noble Francis for the Fifa presidency? I think we could get him 1,057 votes – Jonathan Chester-le-Street.

Your Memory Lane on Nwankwo Kanu’s glorious hat-trick against Chelsea ( Friday’s Football Daily , full email edition) reminded me of the confusion he caused to some Dutch fans sitting in front of us at Dennis Bergkamp’s testimonial, the first game at the Emirates Stadium in 2006. When he scored what would turn out to be the winner against an Ajax legends side, we all erupted in the standard ‘Kanuuuu’ roar, at which point the Dutch fans turned round and asked us, with real concern, why we were booing him. I don’t think they were entirely convinced by our explanation – David Madden.

title: Why is Wilcox in line of fire from Man Utd fans?
text:
As the clock ticked down during Manchester United 's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday, the home fans made it clear what they thought about director of football Jason Wilcox.

Singing his name along with an obscenity, the message was brutal and to the point. It was sung by a majority of the United supporters, and on more than one occasion.

It came less than two weeks after United defender Lisandro Martinez had launched a blistering attack on the club's hierarchy for not strengthening the squad, with a particular message for Wilcox.

"I expect more from our technical director," said Martinez.

Pressure is growing on United boss Michael Carrick after eight games without a win - their worst run since 2015-16 - and two three-goal defeats in a week.

Howe and Nagelsmann high on Man Utd's list if Carrick sacked

End approaching for Carrick but Man Utd fans make clear who they blame

Wilcox is a former England winger who won the Premier League with Blackburn in 1994-95.

He joined United in April 2024 - initially as technical director after 15 months in a similar role at Manchester City , where he had previously been in charge of the academy.

At City he worked with current United chief executive Omar Berrada and also Stephen Torpey, who was appointed United's head of academy in August 2025.

When he arrived, it was said by United officials that Wilcox would work across all technical areas of the club to achieve "highest standards of performance" and would be answerable to the sporting director.

That changed the following December, when that sporting director - Dan Ashworth - was sacked amid a difference of opinion over who should replace Erik ten Hag as manager.

Ten months on, a poor series of results and dissatisfaction with transfer business has put Wilcox in the spotlight.

There are some who have sympathy with the position Wilcox finds himself in. The 55-year-old is not in charge of transfer budgets, which are set at a higher level.

Wilcox was also - obviously - not responsible for the injury Manuel Ugarte sustained playing for Uruguay at the World Cup, which wrecked a plan to sell the midfielder in the summer to bolster the transfer budget.

He, too, was powerless to prevent Barcelona backing out of a £26m deal to sign England forward Marcus Rashford.

Both issues affected the amount United could spend in the summer - both on transfer fees and wages.

Wilcox rarely speaks to the media, and a general lack of communication means we don't know why United decided to focus exclusively on strengthening their midfield in the summer, rather than bring in competition at left-back for Luke Shaw and striking support for Benjamin Sesko.

With both players injured, that looks like a major error.

The general consensus is Carrick has been sold badly short, and Wilcox's job title - and the fact he is often photographed with United's new signings and quoted in official press releases - means he is being blamed.

Since arriving at United from Southampton, Wilcox has twice been given very public backing by his bosses.

On the first occasion - around Ruben Amorim's recruitment as successor to Ten Hag - it was Ashworth who lost his job while Wilcox kept his.

Thirteen months later, when Amorim railed publicly against interference around United's formation - identifying Wilcox as one of those responsible - the Portuguese coach went, and Wilcox remained.

Minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe is yet to offer his thoughts on the present crisis engulfing Old Trafford, but the United fans delivered their verdict loud and clear during the match against Bournemouth .

There are many reasons why United find themselves 16th in the Premier League and without a win in their past eight matches, but recruitment is one of the bigger ones - and for that, rightly or wrongly, Wilcox is getting the blame.

Since joining United, Wilcox has given one extensive interview - to the in-house Inside United podcast in October 2025.

A month before that, he spoke at the 40th anniversary gala dinner of United's past players' association.

But he rarely speaks to the media - there are only a couple of instances in the past 12 months of him stopping for the briefest of chats with journalists when he walked past an area they were waiting in to speak to a United player after a game.

After the defeat by Bournemouth , Carrick was asked directly if Wilcox and Berrada should speak directly to supporters.

"It's not for me to say who speaks and who doesn't speak, when they speak, and how they speak," said Carrick.

"I know my role here is to speak to you guys and represent the team and football club as best as I possibly can from this position."

There has never been an opportunity to ask Wilcox about the parameters of his role.

But with Carrick's situation as it is - his popularity intact and his status as a legendary figure at the club secure - the focus is moving to Wilcox.

United fans have made it clear they want him out - but does Ratcliffe feel the same?

title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
author: Mark Townsend
text:
Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze

Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher , the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.

A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze .

The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century . Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.

The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.

Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.

A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”

During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.

The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

The horse that ushered in Manchester United’s tragic arc | Jonathan Wilson
author: Jonathan Wilson
text:
There’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment

And so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester United prepare to sack a manager . Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford. Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth , coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it.

But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth considering whether the manager is really the problem. Could some blame perhaps go to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, or the chief executive, Omar Berrada, the people making the appointments? Or perhaps to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the cost-cutting tax exile and minority shareholder with responsibility for sporting operations? Or to the Glazer family, who plunged the club into debt with a leveraged buyout in 2005 and have since made calamitous decision after calamitous decision, reducing the most successful club in English league history to a mid-table laughing stock with a roof that leaks symbolically ?

title: Martin's fight to get fit for Malaysian GP with MotoGP title at stake
America’s Newest Cycling Team Is Going Large after Breakout Debut Season
author: Jim Cotton
text:
Modern Adventure Pro Cycling is sizing up for 2027 after its breakout debut season.

Last week, George Hincapie’s budding team revealed a flood of new signings that will expand its debut roster of 21 riders to 24 for its sophomore year.

WorldTour veteran Jonas Rutsch, former U.S. national U23 champion Owen Cole, and reigning Australian champion Patrick Eddy all join the team for 2027.

Meanwhile, the exit door has been kept shut. As of late October, no riders have confirmed they will leave the new American team.

Multiple U.S. national champion Quinn Simmons had been repeatedly linked to Hincapie’s ambitious young project. However, the rumor mill has slowed in recent weeks. The 25-year-old’s long-term deal with Lidl-Trek makes any gamble with Modern Adventure seem highly unlikely.

Simmons or not, the arrival of three new riders in 2027 – a 16 percent expansion in the roster – signals clear intent.

In its rookie 2026 season, the team won five times, raced across continents, and saw a marquee invite to Paris-Roubaix.

In 2027, with added financial heft from new co-title sponsor Factor Bikes, Hincapie wants more from a team he hopes to take toward the Tour de France.

“I wanna look back in five, six years from now and go, ‘this is where we started,’” Hincapie told Velo earlier this season. “From basically ‘Bad News Bears’ to building to be one of the best teams in the world.”

Rutsch and Eddy are the household international names of Modern Adventure’s three new signings.

Rutsch spent seven years in the WorldTour and has twice hit the top-11 at Paris-Roubaix.

Eddy rebounded from losing a spot in the WorldTour by outfoxing two Jayco-AlUla riders at Aussie nationals and dominating the Conti circuit with Team Brennan.

Modern Adventure’s biggest hopes might lie with Cole, however.

The 22-year-old Californian won the U23 U.S. road race aged 19, and this year finished top-six in both the national U23 road race and time trial.

Cole spent a year in the UAE Emirates-XRG devo system in 2024 before he reinforced his status as one of USA’s brightest talents in his two years with Team Winston Salem-Flow.

“We’re excited to welcome Owen to the team. He’s a talented young rider with a bright future, and we’re excited to help him develop,” Hincapie said.

“Supporting young, talented American riders is important to us and part of our mission, and we look forward to helping Owen reach the highest level of the sport.”

Cole is the 13th American rider on Modern Adventure’s 24-rider squad for 2027, maintaining its stated mission of having at least a 50 percent American roster.

title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
author: Guardian sport
text:
Bournemouth’s transfer nous puts United to shame, Araújo is winning admirers at Anfield and Suzuki adapts swiftly at Villa

The three Bournemouth goalscorers cost a combined £85m, joining from Vasco da Gama, Middlesbrough, and Porto. The Cherries are smart at investing, far more so than Manchester United , who have wasted a lot of money by failing to look outside the box for players like Rayan, Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson. United may not have the wealth they previously showed in the transfer market but Bournemouth are showing what can be done within a budget and, more importantly, will be able to make a profit on signings. United, however, only know losses as everyone’s price tag diminishes the moment they come through the Old Trafford door. Jason Wilcox and others can point to certain factors that are against them but there are quality signings to be made at the right price if you have the ability to find them. Will Unwin

Match report: Manchester United 0-3 Bournemouth

Will Unwin: Carrick left carrying can for institutional failings

Aston Villa were quite happy to sell Emiliano Martínez but many feared it would be difficult to find an upgrade on the World Cup-winning goalkeeper. They have seemingly done so in the form of the £30m signing Zion Suzuki, who was superb against Manchester City . Nicolas Jackson’s goals stole the headlines but Suzuki’s bounty of saves ensured that Villa were victorious, while also impressing with his distribution. ”He’s ambitious. I think it’s very important, his mentality,” Unai Emery said. “Of course, we need a keeper first to save us in the goal, but as well we need one keeper to try to help us in our buildup. And in buildup, he’s a really fantastic player because he can play short, he can understand where is the superiority to break the opponent’s press. He has qualities to do long ball, getting our players in attack. So, we are very, very impressed how he adapted so quick with us.” WU

Match report: Aston Villa 2-1 Manchester City

Aside from the reaction to the half-time and full-time scores from Old Trafford, the biggest noise at Anfield was generated by Ronald Araújo showing no mercy in his challenges on Malick Yalcouyé and Charalampos Kostoulas. The on-loan Barcelona defender immediately endeared himself to the Kop with his commitment and quality, and was again in commanding form to help Andoni Iraola record his first Premier League home win as Liverpool head coach. “I think we all enjoyed watching Ronald fighting,” said Iraola. “He’s very good in the duels. Even the first goal, he wins two duels in a row and defensively he’s been really, really good. I’m happy for him because I’ve taken him out in the last two games because we needed more offensive things. But he has continued working with no issues and today we needed him more. He has given a very, very good 90 minutes.” Andy Hunter

João Pedro is unlikely to make a swift return after picking up an injury in training. The Chelsea striker missed the defeat to Tottenham and had a scan on Sunday. Xabi Alonso did not sound optimistic after the Spurs game. The expectation is João Pedro will miss this week’s games against Liverpool and Manchester United as a minimum, leaving Alonso with problems in attack. It was strange he did not start Danny Welbeck against Spurs. Chelsea had no focal point and there are questions over their depth. Emmanuel Emegha, another struggling with injury, is yet to play since joining from Strasbourg. It is fair to wonder if selling Nicolas Jackson to Villa was the right move. Chelsea have played two league games without João Pedro this season and have lost both without scoring a goal. Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers are not as effective without him. Jacob Steinberg

Barney Ronay: Glitch in Chelsea’s coding costs Alonso while resurgent Spurs are all systems go

Mikel Arteta says he has been compiling a dossier of evidence of other managers straying outside the technical area after the Arsenal manager was shown a yellow card during the 2-0 win over Everton . It was his second of the season and leaves the Spaniard at risk of suspension if he gets one more, although Arteta suggested he is by no means the worst offender. “There are managers who have the record in the league, 36 times in 10 minutes [they] leave the touchline – no yellows,” he said, naming no names. “I am clipping all of that so I now have a massive storage of images, so if somebody comes to me I can say: ‘I am not in the record yet.’ Somebody else has the record so let’s see. Then it’s 36 yellow cards in 10 minutes for the managers. I don’t know what we are going to do – let’s see.” Ed Aarons

Nico González cost Manchester City £50m when they signed him early in 2025, as part of that January spree as Pep Guardiola tried to arrest the first real slump of his Premier League career. Although he started nine league games that season and 17 last, González made very little impact at the Etihad. He probably wasn’t even the best Nico González in world football, given the Argentinian winger’s performances for Juventus and Atlético. But the Spanish Nico González clearly is a player of substance, his calm in midfield one of the few undoubted positives for Newcastle so far this season. Only Lewis Hall has made more tackles per game than him, he set up Sven Botman’s goal at Coventry , while he’s made more key passes per game than anybody other than Harvey Barnes. At £48m, he may end up representing extremely good value. Jonathan Wilson

title: The Tour de France Has Made Everyone Angry About a Jersey (Again)
author: Jim Cotton
text:
When the Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes revealed their new-look leaders’ jerseys last week, one color caught everybody’s eye.

The iconic white jersey of “best young rider,” last won by Isaac del Toro and Antonia Niedermaier, will get a facelift in 2027.

The typically pearly maillot has been embellished – or some may say, ruined – by an “ultraviolet” purple trim in a nod to the new jersey sponsor, Sanofi. The Paris-based biopharma company has made the lurid purple its “thing,” apparently.

The introduction of “ultraviolet” into the Tour de France palette has become a serious talking point in a cycling world without racing to argue about.

Purple bits are being debated with equal intensity to the 71km of time trialing in the men’s race and a crowning climb – the Puy de Dôme – at the Femmes that might be closed off to crowds.

“A hater has spent years infiltrating ASO and is now taking revenge by ruining one iconic jersey at a time,” is the brilliant title of one Reddit thread on the topic.

Calls of “fashion crimes,” “a Jayco away kit,” and vomit memes are doing the rounds on Twitter / X .

To be fair, not even the mustachioed model looks too impressed in the official marketing shot.

The Tour hasn’t seen this much confab over clothing since … since the last time race organizer ASO made everyone angry with its leader’s apparel.

In 2023, the vert points jersey turned from lime to forest green at the behest of jersey sponsor Škoda.

Couch Peloton has been in protest ever since.

The new maillot blan c of “best young rider” isn’t the only Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes leader’s jersey that will be relaunched next season.

Last week at the official route reveals , ASO revealed tweaked versions of all four of its iconic classification leaders’ jerseys.

The historic yellow, green, polka dot, and white tops have all gotten a refresh for 2027 courtesy of ASO’s new clothing supplier, Castelli.

The Italian brand returns to the Tour for the first time in more than 30 years in 2027. Santini had done the honors since 2022.

Castelli also takes charge of the sewing machine for the ASO-owned Paris-Roubaix, Paris-Nice, Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, and Vuelta a España.

The Tour de France jersey polemica is isolated to just the purple-on-white maillot blanc .

The maillots jaune , verte and à pois haven’t been messed with enough to catch public ire.

In a recent statement, Castelli brand manager Steve Smith paid tribute to the heft of the Tour’s classification jerseys.

“Producing the maillot jaune represents the highest possible honor. We wanted these jerseys to be truly special. That is why every micro-detail stems from our deep reverence for what they represent to the sport and the riders who earn them,” Smith said.

“Beyond pushing performance and aerodynamics, every single feature was crafted to honor that legacy.”

Some may argue purple is not a part of the Tour de France white jersey legacy.

title: Antonelli superb and Leclerc close to perfect - driver ratings
text:
Championship leader Kimi Antonelli sealed his ninth victory of the season with victory at the United States Grand Prix in Austin.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc was second and Red Bull's Max Verstappen third.

Mercedes' Antonelli, 20, can become the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history if he finishes ninth or higher at the Mexico City Grand Prix next weekend.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Texas.

A superb weekend under the added pressure of having his first opportunity to seal the championship. Produced an outstanding lap for pole and then controlled the race beautifully, making the one-stop work while many around him needed two.

Very close to a perfect weekend himself. Fastest in both Friday practice sessions, qualified fourth and then raced brilliantly in his Ferrari to second, including late passes on Lando Norris and Max Verstappen.

Quick all weekend and put the Red Bull on the front row, but the poor start immediately made his race more difficult. Recovered well despite problems with the car and still came away with a sixth consecutive podium.

Another strong weekend but behind team-mate Leclerc for the majority of it. Fastest in final practice, only narrowly behind Leclerc in qualifying and fought his way back to fourth after Ferrari committed to the two-stop strategy.

Recovered well from eighth on the grid but qualifying should have been better as his quickest Q3 lap was deleted for track limits. McLaren's decision to leave him out on ageing tyres cost him late on, so fifth was not entirely of his own making.

An excellent turnaround after struggling badly with the Red Bull during practice. Qualified a superb third, ran strongly in the race and eventually finished sixth despite throttle mapping problems and moving aside for team-mate Verstappen.

A fairly subdued weekend by the McLaren man's standards. Seventh in qualifying and seventh in the race, although the first-lap battle with George Russell went against him and the stewards decided the Mercedes driver was at fault.

A disappointing weekend given what the other Mercedes achieved. Admitted both of his Q3 laps were poor and then picked up a five-second time penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage in his battle with Piastri, eventually finishing eighth.

Another quietly excellent weekend from Lawson. Racing Bulls sacrificed a proper Q3 attempt to preserve tyres for Sunday and he converted ninth on the grid into ninth at the finish to score again.

Probably extracted just about everything available from the Alpine. Missed Q3 but fought his way back into the points after an early dice with Haas' Oliver Bearman.

Antonelli wins in US but has to wait to secure title

Antonelli delivers 'the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet'

Another solid if unspectacular weekend for the Audi driver. Just missed Q3 and spent Sunday on the fringes of the points before eventually finishing 11th.

Reaching Q3 was an excellent effort after admitting team-mate Lawson had been quicker than him for much of the weekend. A power-unit penalty dropped him from ninth to 14th on the grid and he recovered a couple of positions to 12th.

A much better weekend than 13th suggests. Produced what he described as one of his best qualifying laps before helping team-mate Hulkenberg with a tow, then recovered from 21st on the grid after an enormous power-unit penalty.

Out in Q1 and again lacked the pace team-mate Bearman had shown earlier in the weekend. Gained places at the start and Haas eventually prioritised his undamaged car, but 14th was all he could manage.

Started from the pit lane after Aston Martin made changes to the car and fitted additional power unit components, so 15th represented a reasonable recovery. Beat team-mate Fernando Alonso to the flag after a weekend where neither car looked particularly competitive.

Getting the Aston Martin into Q2 was encouraging and penalties initially promoted him to 12th on the grid. But he went backwards on Sunday and contact with Williams' Alex Albon didn't help as he eventually finished behind Stroll after a slow pit stop.

Williams knew this circuit would expose the weaknesses of their car and that proved to be the case. Qualified behind team-mate Carlos Sainz but at least he recovered to lead the team home after an eventful opening part of the race.

A mistake late in his final qualifying lap contributed to a Q1 exit on a weekend when Williams were already struggling badly. Finished behind Albon and never looked capable of rescuing points from a difficult weekend.

Beat team-mate Valtteri Bottas in qualifying despite suffering an energy-recovery issue on his final lap. But Cadillac simply didn't have competitive pace at their home race, and P19 was a fairly anonymous result.

Qualified last before eventually retiring late enough to trigger the final virtual safety car. There wasn't much evidence across the weekend that Cadillac had the performance to achieve anything significant.

Qualified 14th but a 10-place power-unit penalty left the Alpine driver effectively starting from the back. His retirement meant there was little opportunity to turn the weekend around.

There had been real promise after he led Haas throughout Friday and initially looked quick enough for 13th in qualifying before losing his lap to track limits. Sunday unravelled with contact, a penalty and damage before he eventually retired.

title: Antonelli delivers 'the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet'
text:
The race that took Kimi Antonelli to the brink of a record-breaking world championship was, in the words of his Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff, "the best he has delivered so far" and "the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet".

The 20-year-old Italian's victory in the United States Grand Prix puts him in an impregnable position.

Antonelli is so far ahead in the points that the only way he could not win the title in Mexico City next weekend is if either his team-mate George Russell or Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton win the race. Even then, Antonelli will guarantee the title if he finishes ninth, or 10th if it's Hamilton.

He arrived here thanks to one of the most dominant victories of the season, in a car in which Russell could finish only eighth, albeit hampered by a five-second penalty.

While Russell was toiling and failing to pass McLaren's Oscar Piastri, Antonelli was operating on another level entirely, as he has so often this season.

"Exceptional," Wolff said, "and I think he's outperformed the car."

Antonelli wins in US but has to wait to secure title

Antonelli superb and Leclerc close to perfect - driver ratings

Antonelli came to Austin already in a strong position in the championship, knowing he would clinch the title if he won with Russell finishing lower than eighth and Hamilton lower than fourth.

He achieved his part of the bargain but Russell and Hamilton did just enough to keep things alive until this coming weekend. Russell was eighth and Hamilton fourth.

Some drivers tighten up when they get this close to achieving their lifetime's ambition. Not Antonelli. He said he was going to treat this like any other weekend, but it wasn't just talk. It's exactly what he did.

"He comes in," Wolff told BBC Sport after the race, in a conversation after finishing his official news conference, "sits on my chair, feet up, and keeps chatting away and saying: 'This is so funny. I'm not thinking about the championship at all.' And in a kind of youngish excitement, almost like it's surreal. And that's why it's not so important."

Did Wolff think that was because Antonelli's lead was so large that he had no need to feel any pressure, or was it innate?

"The advantage helps," he said. "But it's also innate in him and I don't think that it's something to be trained for. He's not over-thinking it."

Wolff's claim about this being Antonelli's best performance so far might surprise anyone who watched him win his home grand prix at Monza from 19th on the grid.

When this was pointed out, Wolff replied: "My problem is that I don't remember past races. So now you're saying Monza was actually also pretty good, obviously with the advantage of the home crowd and seeing all these tifosi that were a little bit confused, wearing red, and an Italian with the Mercedes outfit up on the podium. And I think we're going to see more Kimi caps, Mercedes caps next year.

"So both of them were pretty good. But the headline that this is the best we can keep."

Antonelli agreed. "Monza, we clearly had the fastest car," he said. "We were just super quick, so of course it was incredibly special coming from the back. But it was also a track where it was relatively easy to overtake, and we were so quick.

"Definitely, Monza was a super-special one, and one that I will remember forever. But this one probably, in terms of execution, was better, because the way we built up and the way we built the performance throughout the weekend was very good."

Mercedes went to Austin with both cars in the new upgraded specification that had proved unconvincing, to say the least, when it made its debut in Malaysia two races ago.

There, Wolff said he thought it had made the car 0.3secs per lap slower. The team split the cars in Singapore to try to understand the package better, and then used it on both cars in Austin. Antonelli stuck it on pole and dominated the race. Russell's performance looked more like the one the car produced in Malaysia.

"The update we put on the car is difficult to operate," Wolff said. "And Kimi landed it.

"Maybe it's a bit harsh to say but I think his driving style just glues with the car. We saw that in qualifying yesterday where on his last lap he could have been another 0.15-0.2 secs up. And on the other side George just struggled so much. And I believe this is because the operational window of the car is so difficult."

When Antonelli clinches the title, he will become the first Italian to do so since Alberto Ascari in 1953. It's a remarkable statistic for a country which is so engrained in the sport, and it certainly resonates with his compatriots.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "As an Italian, wow, we need to go back to Ascari, the names that they created the inspiration for all of us. To see an Italian achieving this level of performance and results in Formula 1, that's particularly thrilling, as an Italian person in motorsport."

Stella's answer continued into an area that begins to explain the way in which he has proved so superior to Russell this year.

"Going more into the technical, and specifically this season, Kimi is a very interesting one to look at, because he pretty much attacks all the times," Stella said.

"You see how often he's just going off track, and you see his onboard (camera), he's pretty aggressive. But at the same time, this seems to be not only kind of an aggressive driving, or an attacking driving, but effective.

"And if we think how much we talk in these media sessions about the cars being difficult to drive consistently fast, it should be recognised how much he's been able to harness his driving style with what is required of the cars.

"But at the same time, almost contradicting what I'm saying, when is the time to bring home the result, he's been able to do it.

"So he's the deserving leader of this championship. He's writing an important piece of history for motorsport, because once he achieves the championship, he will be the youngest."…
